chapter_theme: The second half of the Aaychiyar Kuravai: the herdswomen sing Maayavan's herd-village play with Pinnai, set their ring by the gods they enact, praise the three crowned kings in the ulvari as bearers of Vishnu's deeds, address Maal with the paradox of the cosmic god bound and thieving, define ear, eye and tongue by his praise, and close by asking the god to end the cattle's distress and the Pandya's drum to win daily, on the very day that king's verdict has killed Kovalan.

cast.role: the herdswomen of the Madurai outskirts, led by the old herdswoman, who dance and sing the kuravai
Maal (Thirumaal, Narayana), the god praised in the kuravai, addressed in the second-person stanzas

silappathikaram:17:79-81.reading: The herd girls open the kuravai song: if the wonder-working one who churned the sea with a snake for rope came among their cattle, would they not hear the sweet aambal-mode flute at his lips?
silappathikaram:17:79-81.nuance: The cosmic deed (the churning) and the herd-village wish (his flute among 'our cattle', நம் ஆனுள்) are set in one line pair; each stanza of this song names one deed of Maayavan and one flute mode (கொன்றை, ஆம்பல், முல்லை), so the song is also a demonstration of modes.

silappathikaram:17:82-86.reading: The third stanza wishes for the mullai flute of the one who broke the kurundu tree on the hill slope, and the girls turn to sing the beauty of Pinnai who danced with the lord of the Yamuna ford.
silappathikaram:17:82-86.nuance: Lines 85-86 are the turn of the song from Maayavan to Pinnai (பின்னை அணிநிறம் பாடுகேம் யாம்), which the next three stanzas carry out.

silappathikaram:17:87-90.reading: The girls ask what words could tell the form of him who hid the garment as Pinnai's soft grace swayed, and the face of her who wilts as he plays on.
silappathikaram:17:87-90.nuance: The stanza is built as a chiasmus: each half-line answers the other, his form and her face, so the lovers' play is shown as mutual. The garment hidden (அறுவை யொளித்தான்) is the god's prank at the river.

silappathikaram:17:91-94.reading: The girls ask what to call the self-possession of her who stole the heart of the trickster in the Yamuna, and the form of the trickster who took her self-possession and her bangles.
silappathikaram:17:91-94.nuance: நிறை, a woman's self-containment, is here lost and won in a game: she takes his heart and he takes her நிறை and bangles. Who seized whose heart turns on how கவர்ந்தாள் is construed; the reading taken is that she captured his.

silappathikaram:17:95-98.reading: The girls sing that the maiden, robbed of garment and bangles, hid her face in her hands, and that he, seeing the hidden face, suffered infatuation.
silappathikaram:17:95-98.nuance: The trickster ends caught himself: மைய லுழந்தான், he laboured in infatuation. The modesty of the hidden face (கையி லொளித்தாள் முகம்) is what defeats him.

silappathikaram:17:99-102.reading: The dance's arrangement is told through the myth: Pinnai stands at the left of the sea-coloured one who hid the sun with his discus and at the right of his moon-fair elder, others keep her measure, and Narada, versed in the old Veda, plucks the strings in their first order.
silappathikaram:17:99-102.nuance: Part 1 of the kaathai gave each girl the name of a god and a note of the scale; this block names their places in the ring by the gods they play. 'Hid the sun with the discus' (கதிர்திகிரி யான்மறைத்த) alludes to a Krishna story the line does not tell.

silappathikaram:17:103-106.reading: The second stanza turns the ring: Pinnai is now at the right of the peacock-necked Maayavan and the left of his elder, and Narada among the musicians plucks the strings in the tuned measure.
silappathikaram:17:103-106.nuance: Left and right are exchanged from the stanza before, so the pair of stanzas records the dancers moving round. கயிலெருத்தம் கோட்டிய (line 105) is a rare phrase for Pinnai's bent neck.

silappathikaram:17:107-110.reading: The dancers praise the kuravai danced on the dusty common by Maayavan with his elder and bangled Pinnai, the herd girls' hair garlands slipping and Asodhai praising with joined hands, as fitting.
silappathikaram:17:107-110.nuance: The mythic kuravai of Ayarpadi is the model the Madurai herdswomen are copying, so praising it praises their own dance; the herd mother Asodhai worships the child-god she raises.

silappathikaram:17:111-113.reading: One of the women calls all of them to praise the god whose mount is the bird, taking up the ulvari tune.
silappathikaram:17:111-113.event: The herdswomen call one another to praise the bird-riding god in the ulvari mode.

silappathikaram:17:114-117.reading: The first ulvari stanza says the hill's pearl string, the sea's pearl string and the necklace of the king of the gods are on the chest of the Pandya, and that the one who wears the gods' king's necklace, they say, grazed the herds at Dvaraka and broke the kurundu tree.
silappathikaram:17:114-117.nuance: The 'inner vari' (உள்வரி) has the singers take on another person: the Pandya is hailed with Krishna's herd-deeds, so king and god are fused. The fusion is ironic in the story, since this king has that day ordered Kovalan's death.

silappathikaram:17:118-121.reading: The second stanza hails the Chola Valavan of walled Puhar, who carved his tiger on the Himalaya and ruled the earth, as the one, they say, who bears the golden discus as weapon.
silappathikaram:17:118-121.nuance: Each of the three crowns is given a mark of Vishnu: the Chola the discus (திகிரி), as the Pandya the herd-deeds and the Chera the churning. The refrain doubles line 120.

silappathikaram:17:122-125.reading: The third stanza hails the Chera of prosperous Vanchi, who went into the sea and threw down the ageless kadambu, as the one who, they say, churned the sea with his stone-strong arms.
silappathikaram:17:122-125.nuance: The Chera's sea-raid is renamed with the churning of the ocean (கடல்கடைந்தான்), the deed this song gave Maayavan at line 79. The stanza names only 'the Chera, king of kings', not a particular Cheralathan.

silappathikaram:17:126-129.reading: Addressing the lotus-naveled god, the women say that he who once churned the sea with the north mountain for staff and Vasuki for rope had the same hand bound by Asodhai's churning cord, and ask whether this is his maayam, for it bewilders them.
silappathikaram:17:126-129.nuance: Cosmic churning and the herd mother's churning rope (கடைகயிறு, the tool the old herdswoman carried in at line 9) meet in one hand. The refrain மாயமோ மருட்கைத்தே asks rather than explains.

silappathikaram:17:130-133.reading: The women tell the god that, while the hosts of gods praised him as the final truth, he swallowed the whole world without hunger, and the same mouth ate stolen butter from the hanging pot.
silappathikaram:17:130-133.nuance: Again the god's greatest act and his smallest theft share one organ, here the mouth; 'without hunger' (உறுபசியொன் றின்றியே) marks the swallowing of the world as play, not need.

claims.claim: the gods worship Maal as the ultimate reality

silappathikaram:17:134-137.reading: The women tell Thirumaal that with his two red-lotus feet he strode the three worlds so their darkness lifted, that the same feet walked as envoy for the Pandavas, and that he became a lion and killed the foe.
silappathikaram:17:134-137.nuance: The stanza joins the cosmic stride to a humble errand, the envoy's walk, on the same feet (நடந்தஅடி repeated).

silappathikaram:17:138-142.reading: Turning to the third person, the women ask what ear it is that has not heard the glory of the hero who, after his feet had spanned the three worlds in two strides, went to the forest with his brother and destroyed old Lanka, and of Thirumaal.
silappathikaram:17:138-142.nuance: The 'praise in the third person' (படர்க்கைப் பரவல்) defines each sense organ by its devotion: an ear that has not heard his praise is no ear. The stanza ties the Vamana stride to the Rama story as one person's deeds.

claims.claim: an ear that does not hear Thirumaal's praise is no ear

silappathikaram:17:143-147.reading: The women ask what eye it is that has not seen the great dark one, the god of the lotus navel who holds all the worlds, whose eyes, feet, hands and mouth are red, and what eyes are those that blink while looking at him.
silappathikaram:17:143-147.nuance: Line 147 sharpens line 146: even an eye that sees him is faulted if it blinks, since the gods do not blink; the devotee should look unblinking.

claims.claim: an eye that has not seen Maal is no eye

silappathikaram:17:148-159.reading: The women ask what tongue it is that does not praise or name Narayana, who overcame Kamsa's deceit and walked as envoy to the hundred for the Pandavas, then close the kuravai: may the god it praised take away the distress fallen on their cattle, and may the drum of the Pandya, who broke the crown of the thunder-armed god, bring victory day after day.
silappathikaram:17:148-159.nuance: The close returns to the omens that opened the kaathai (the curd that would not set, the bulls' tears): the dance was a rite to avert them. Its last wish, victory for the Pandya's drum, is set on the day that king's verdict has killed Kovalan, so the blessing turns to irony; the next kaathai brings the news. The god is asked to protect the herd, and the king's fate is asked of his drum.
silappathikaram:17:148-159.event: The herdswomen end the kuravai praying that the god remove the cattle's distress and that the Pandya's drum bring victory.

claims.claim: a tongue that does not say Narayana's name is no tongue
the god praised in the kuravai will take away the distress fallen on the cattle

links.note: The herdswomen pray that the Pandya's drum bring victory day after day; the same day that king's verdict has killed Kovalan, and the next morning he names himself the thief and dies.
links.teaches: The closing blessing is the stock wish of a herders' song, but placed on the day the sceptre has bent it becomes a prayer for a king already doomed, so the reader hears the epic's justice theme inside a rite meant only to save the cattle.

links.note: Kalittokai 104 ends its herders' kuravai by praising the god of the ancient bright discus and wishing that the world take the one word of the Pandya with the thunder-loud drum; the epic's kuravai to the discus-holder (கதிர்திகிரி, line 99) ends in the same wish for the Pandya's drum.
links.teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam mullai close, god first and then the Pandya's drum, but moves the kuravai from the joy after the bull-catch to a rite against ill omens, so the inherited blessing now carries dread rather than celebration.

gains.a: the epic's close is shown to be a set form of the Madurai herders' kuravai, not Ilango's invention, which makes its irony a turn on a known convention
gains.b: the Kalittokai's conventional wish for the Pandya is shown to be one that a story could test: the epic sets it on the day the same dynasty's justice fails

links.note: Patitruppattu 11 likens Cheralathan's sea-raid and felling of the guarded kadambu to Murugan cutting down Sur in the sea; the epic's herdswomen tell the same Chera deed and say he churned the sea, Vishnu's deed.
links.teaches: Both poets lift the Chera's kadambu raid into a god's sea-deed, but each picks the god of its own setting: the Patitruppattu's war poem chooses Murugan, the herders' kuravai chooses Maal, so the same royal memory is divinised differently by genre.

gains.a: the epic's bare 'the Chera who threw down the kadambu' gains the Sangam record of who did it and how it was praised, while the epic itself does not name Neduncheralathan
gains.b: the Patitruppattu's comparison gains a later witness showing the kadambu raid still famous enough to be sung by Pandya herdswomen beside the other two crowns

links.note: Kural 9 says a head that does not bow at the feet of the eight-qualitied one is as useless as a sense organ without its power; the kuravai asks what ear it is that has not heard Thirumaal's praise, and goes on to the eye and the tongue.
links.teaches: The couplet's simile, an organ without its function, becomes in the kuravai a definition carried through ear, eye and tongue, so the claim that the body's parts exist for worship is spelled out organ by organ and bound to one named god.

gains.a: the epic's refrain gains a recognised ethical form: it is the Kural's argument that an organ is defined by its proper act, applied to devotion
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed god and single organ gain a sung extension, where the same test is applied to each sense and given a sectarian object

links.note: Paripadal 3 says the god is everything and the essence within everything and calls him one full of maayam (மாயமார் அனையை); the kuravai asks whether the churner of the sea bound by Asodhai's churning rope is maayam, for it bewilders.
links.teaches: The hymn treats the god's maayam as a doctrine to be stated, his being all things at once, while the herdswomen meet it as an unanswered question in a domestic scene, so the same paradox is shown both as learned theology and as village wonder.

gains.a: the kuravai's question gains an answer it does not give: the hymn's account of why one god can be both the cosmic churner and a bound child
gains.b: the hymn's abstract claim gains a concrete case, a single hand that churned the ocean and was tied with a butter-churn's cord

new_concepts.gloss: music: the lute, melody, mode and the sounds compared to them
new_concepts.label_source: the verses name the flute and its modes (ஆம்பலந் தீங்குழல் line 81, முல்லையந் தீங்குழல் line 84) and the plucked strings (நரம்புளர்வார் lines 102, 106); id as used in the Pattupattu and Valayapathi marks

new_concepts.gloss: dance as an art and a performance, with its forms, costumes and rules
new_concepts.label_source: the verses' word: தாதெருமன் றத்தாடுங் குரவை line 110, ஆடிய line 85; id as declared in the Silappathikaram ch007 marks

new_concepts.gloss: the herders' round dance with linked hands, danced by the girls and the young men after the bull-catch
new_concepts.label_source: the kaathai's own word: கோத்த குரவையுள் line 154, குரவையோ line 110 (id as declared in the Kalittokai marks)

source_issues: Lines 146-147 spell the refrain கண்ணென்ண கண்ணே with ண where the parallel refrains have என்ன (செவி என்ன செவியே, நாவென்ன நாவே); likely a typing slip for கண்ணென்ன.
The god's consort is spelt both பின்னை (lines 85, 105, 107) and பிஞ்ஞை (line 101) within the kaathai.
